Section.Description: This section summarizes the environmental fate/exposure of this chemical, including the natural and artificial sources of the chemical as a pollutant, its environmental fate, biodegradation, abiotic degradation, bioconcentration, etc.

StringWithMarkup.String: Oxythioquinox's production may result in its release to the environment through various waste streams; its use as a fungicide and acaricide will result in its direct release to the environment. However, oxythioquinox is not currently (March 2005) registered for use as a pesticide in the US. If released to air, a vapor pressure of 2.0X10-7 mm Hg at 20 °C indicates oxythioquionx will exist in both the vapor and particulate phases in the ambient atmosphere. Vapor-phase oxythioquinox will be degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals; the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 4.8 days. Particulate-phase oxythioquinox will be removed from the atmosphere by wet and dry deposition. Oxythioquinox may be susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight based on experiments that found that it decomposed in benzene solution upon irradiation with long wavelengths (>290 nm). If released to soil, oxythioquinox is expected to have slight to no mobility based upon Koc values ranging from 2,300 to 28,235. Volatilization from moist soil surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process based upon an estimated Henry's Law constant of 6.2X10-8 atm-cu m/mole. A photolysis rate of 0.014 per day has been reported for oxythioquinox on soil, which corresponds to a half-life of 50 days. Field dissipation half-lives of 2.0-3.6 days have been reported for oxythioquinox in two sandy loam soils. If released into water, oxythioquinox is expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment based upon the Koc values. Volatilization from water surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process based upon this compound's estimated Henry's Law constant. An estimated BCF of 160 suggests the potential for bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is high. Hydrolysis half-lives of 10 days, 80 hours, and 225 minutes have been reported for oxythioquinox at 22 °C and pH 4, 7, and 9, respectively. A photolysis rate of 1.260 per day has been reported for oxythioquinox in water, which corresponds to a half-life of 0.5 day. Occupational exposure to oxythioquinox may occur through inhalation and dermal contact with this pesticide during and after its application or at workplaces where oxythioquinox is produced. Available monitoring data are limited; however, the data suggest that the general population may have been exposed to oxythioquinox by the ingestion of some fruits. (SRC)

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.
